title: Lords of the Cosmos
author: Arjun Khemani and Logan Chipkin
length: 9 chapters, with introduction and reading list
openingText: The universe was utterly monotonous for most of its history until only a few hundred years ago, containing just a few kinds of objects—stars, planets, black holes, and little else. The dawn of life on Earth at last brought genuine novelty into the world, but mankind contributed very little to it until the Enlightenment during the sixteenth, seventeenth, and eighteenth centuries. For most of our history, our cultures were static. Then, with the philosophical advances of the Enlightenment, the West figured out how to make continuous progress—it became a dynamic society. While the Enemies of Civilization had dominated static societies of the past, they continue to hamper progress to this day. All of them fail to appreciate that problems are due to lack of knowledge—and, therefore, that speed, creativity, and freedom are necessary for progress, rather than political and intellectual tyranny, reducing resource consumption, and ridding the Earth of humanity. As we continue to solve problems, we will come to dominate the entire cosmos. Welcome to the Anthropocene.
about:
Lords of the Cosmos began as the script for Arjun Khemani's documentary of the same name, written with Logan Chipkin and drawn heavily from David Deutsch's The Beginning of Infinity. Its argument is that the universe, and then human society, stayed almost unchanged for nearly all of its history, until the Enlightenment discovered how to make progress continuous.

The first six chapters move from the cosmic 'Great Monotony' through Sparta and Athens and the Enlightenment to the ideas the authors call the enemies of civilization. They end with Deutsch's principle of optimism: every evil is caused by a lack of knowledge. Chapter 7, the book's main addition to the film, retells the history of everything as a series of bottlenecks in knowledge, from the Big Bang and the first replicator to language, money, the scientific revolution and the universal computer.

Chapter 8 looks forward to immortality, artificial general intelligence, anarcho-capitalism, Taking Children Seriously and the universal constructor. Chapter 9 closes on the Anthropocene and the place of people in the cosmos, and an organized reading list follows. The authors write as advocates. Their politics are libertarian, and they name socialism, environmentalism and the degrowth movement among the enemies of progress. Read for a compact, openly opinionated tour of Deutsch's worldview, and for the arguments you would want to test.

whyItMatters.title: Static and dynamic societies
whyItMatters.body:
The book contrasts Sparta, which suppressed creativity in its young, with Periclean Athens, which tolerated new ideas, and asks why stagnation was the human norm for so long. Deutsch's distinction between the two kinds of society organizes the whole history that follows.

Today: Ask which institutions around you reward a new idea and which ones punish it.

whyItMatters.title: Optimism as a claim about physics
whyItMatters.body:
Chapter 6 treats optimism as an argument, not a mood: any transformation the laws of nature allow can be achieved with the right knowledge. The authors use it to answer resignation about poverty, disease and death.

Today: Pessimism about technology and the future is a common public stance, and this chapter argues directly against it.

whyItMatters.title: A history told through knowledge
whyItMatters.body:
Chapter 7 tells the story of the universe as a sequence of leaps: replicators, eukaryotes, multicellular life, universal explainers, language, property, money, science and computation. Each section asks what new kind of knowledge appeared and what it made possible.

Today: The chapter on the universal computer reads as background to current debates about artificial intelligence.

angleCards.title: Map it to Deutsch
angleCards.text: The authors call The Beginning of Infinity their main source. Track which ideas come straight from Deutsch and which are the authors' own extensions, especially in economics and politics.
angleCards.angleObjective: I want to distinguish what Lords of the Cosmos takes from David Deutsch's The Beginning of Infinity from the authors' own political and economic conclusions.

angleCards.title: Argue with the enemies list
angleCards.text: Chapter 5 names socialism, environmentalism and degrowth as enemies of civilization. Read the strongest form of each position against the authors' case and decide where the argument holds.
angleCards.angleObjective: I want to test the arguments in Lords of the Cosmos against socialism, environmentalism and degrowth by comparing them with the strongest versions of those positions.

angleCards.title: Follow the bottlenecks
angleCards.text: Read Chapter 7 as one argument. At each stage, from abiogenesis to the steam engine, note what knowledge was missing and what broke the bottleneck.
angleCards.angleObjective: I want to follow the knowledge-centered history in Chapter 7 of Lords of the Cosmos, noting at each stage what knowledge was missing and what made progress possible.

angleCards.title: Weigh the future
angleCards.text: Chapter 8 predicts immortality, creative AGI and a stateless society. Separate what the authors claim is physically possible from what they claim is desirable.
angleCards.angleObjective: I want to examine the predictions in Chapter 8 of Lords of the Cosmos, separating claims about what is physically possible from claims about what is desirable.

cast.name: Arjun Khemani
cast.description: Made the documentary Lords of the Cosmos, whose script is the core of this book, and decided in 2024 to bring the ideas of The Beginning of Infinity to a television-like audience. He dedicates the book to David Deutsch, 'whose explanations transformed my world.'

cast.name: Logan Chipkin
cast.description: Collaborated with Khemani on the script and on the book's expansion. He is President and Cofounder of Conjecture Institute, the book's publisher, and edits the Bold Conjectures series.

cast.name: David Deutsch
cast.description: Oxford physicist and author of The Beginning of Infinity, which the authors call a masterpiece and their main inspiration. His ideas supply the book's framework: people as universal explainers, static versus dynamic societies, the principle of optimism, and the claim that all evils are caused by a lack of knowledge.

cast.name: Karl Popper
cast.description: The philosopher of science whose account of knowledge as conjecture and criticism underlies Deutsch's work and this book. His call to 'fight for a better world' instead of prophesying evil opens Chapter 6.

cast.name: Sparta and Athens
cast.description: The book's models of a static and a dynamic society. Fifth-century Sparta trained obedient citizen-soldiers and resisted change. Athens under Pericles built the Parthenon and was home to Socrates, Plato, Herodotus and Thucydides.

cast.name: Universal explainers
cast.description: Deutsch's term for entities that can create an explanation of anything that can be understood. The authors argue that people alone can cause any transformation the laws of physics allow, which makes them, in the title's phrase, lords of the cosmos.
